threads.thread_goal: Align on MVP scope, success metrics, and responsibilities.

messages.text: Welcome to the Unified Self-Service Support Portal project kickoff. We have 30 days to launch an MVP that reduces inbound calls and improves customer experience. Let's start by aligning on scope and success metrics. I've outlined the core deliverables: responsive web UI, knowledge base, search/FAQ integration, content governance, analytics dashboard, and support team training. We need to lock in what's in vs. out for day 30. Please review A1 (MVP Scope and Metrics) and T1 (Define MVP feature set) and share your initial thoughts on what we can realistically deliver.

Good framing. I've reviewed the scope and I think we should be explicit about what's NOT in the MVP. Advanced personalization, multi-language support, and custom integrations beyond auth/CRM should go to post-launch backlog. For success metrics, I'd propose: (1) 40% call deflection within first month, (2) 70% portal adoption among customers who receive in-queue promotion, (3) zero critical accessibility gaps at launch. These are measurable and tied to the business outcome. Let me know if these feel right or if we need to adjust.

The metrics make sense from a content perspective. I want to flag that 70% adoption assumes we have strong in-queue messaging and that the portal is genuinely easy to use. From my side, I can commit to having 25 FAQs and 10 how-to articles ready by day 20, but that depends on getting clear call driver data from 6370 early. Also, do we have a decision on whether we're launching with a knowledge base search or just browsable FAQs? That affects content structure.

Good catch. Search is in scope for MVP—it's a core deflection lever. We'll implement basic keyword search on the FAQ page (T9). 6370, can you get us the top 20 call reasons by EOD tomorrow? That unblocks T2 and feeds into 561463's content planning. 75507, we also need the IA and wireframes to be ready by day 5 so we can validate the structure with the team before 448709 starts building.

I can pull the top call reasons from our logs. I'll have that list ready tomorrow. One thing though—I want to make sure the FAQ answers are actually clear and match how we explain things on the phone. I've seen content that looks good on paper but confuses customers. I'll review the drafts once 561463 has them written.

Day 5 for IA and wireframes is tight but doable. I'll start with the user flows for search, FAQ browsing, and contact escalation. I'm assuming we're keeping the visual style simple and accessible—no heavy animations or custom fonts that might slow things down. Should I align with 561463 on tone and style guidelines before I finalize the wireframes?

Yes, let's sync. I'll draft A3 (Content Style and Accessibility Guide) by day 3 so you have the tone and accessibility rules locked in. That way your wireframes and my content are aligned from the start.

Understood. I'll be ready to start front-end build once the wireframes are approved. Just to confirm—are we using the existing auth system for login, or is this a public portal? And do we need to integrate with the CRM for anything beyond pulling customer data?

Good questions. The portal is public—no login required for FAQ/search. But we'll integrate with auth for optional account features (saved articles, feedback) in a future phase. For MVP, it's read-only public access. CRM integration is for analytics only—tracking which articles are viewed and estimated deflection. I'll detail this in A5 (Technical Architecture) by day 4. 448709, once you have the wireframes, you can start the responsive front-end build in parallel with my architecture work.

I want to circle back on the success metrics. I think we should also add a fourth metric: support team satisfaction with the portal's usefulness. If agents don't trust the content or find it hard to reference during calls, adoption will stall. Can we add a quick post-launch survey for the support team? That's low effort and gives us feedback for iteration.

Solid point. Let's add that as a secondary metric—not a go/no-go, but important for post-launch iteration. So our primary success metrics are: (1) 40% call deflection, (2) 70% adoption, (3) zero critical accessibility gaps. Secondary: support team satisfaction score of 7+/10. Does everyone agree on these? If so, I'll document them in A1 and we can move to decision D2.
Agreed. Those metrics are clear and achievable. I'm ready to commit to the content side.
Works for me. I'll make sure the UX supports those metrics—especially the accessibility piece.
Looks good. I'll make sure the FAQs address the real pain points so we actually hit that deflection target.
Confirmed. Ready to build.

Excellent. Now let's lock in the MVP feature list. Based on the project brief, the MVP includes: (1) responsive web UI with home, FAQ, and search pages, (2) knowledge base with 25+ FAQs and 10+ how-to articles, (3) search and filtering on FAQ page, (4) basic analytics dashboard, (5) support team training materials. NOT in MVP: advanced personalization, multi-language, custom integrations, user accounts, feedback forms. Everyone clear? This is D1—approve the MVP feature list and park non-MVP items.

I'd suggest we add one thing to MVP: a simple 'contact support' button on every page that escalates to the call centre if the FAQ doesn't help. That's a quick win for UX and reduces frustration. It's just a button + email integration, which we already have. Should take 448709 maybe 2 hours. Worth it?
Good idea. 448709, can you estimate that? If it's truly 2 hours and doesn't block other work, let's add it. Otherwise, it goes to post-launch.
I can do it. Should be straightforward—just a form that sends an email to the support queue. I'll add it to T5 (front-end build).

Perfect. So D1 is now: MVP includes responsive web UI, knowledge base (25+ FAQs, 10+ how-to), search/filtering, contact escalation button, basic analytics, and support training. Non-MVP items logged for post-launch backlog. Everyone confirm?
Confirmed. I'll update A1 with the final feature list and metrics.
Confirmed. Let's move fast on the call driver analysis and IA so we don't lose momentum.

threads.thread_goal: Prioritise top call drivers and confirm initial FAQ set.

messages.text: I've pulled the top call drivers from our logs over the last 3 months. Here's what I found: (1) billing and invoice questions (18%), (2) password resets and account access (15%), (3) shipping and delivery status (14%), (4) product returns and refunds (12%), (5) subscription changes (11%), (6) technical troubleshooting (10%), (7) general product info (8%), (8) payment methods (7%), (9) order tracking (5%). I've mapped these to draft FAQ topics in A2 (Top Call Drivers and FAQ Mapping). The top 5 categories account for 70% of inbound calls, so if we nail those, we should hit our deflection target. I've also noted which topics need input from other teams—like billing and subscriptions might need product/finance review.

This is really helpful. I can start drafting FAQs for the top 5 categories right away. But I need to flag: some of these topics (like billing, returns, subscriptions) require accurate, up-to-date info that changes frequently. I'll need clear ownership and a review process. For example, who owns the billing FAQ? Is it finance, product, or support? And how often do we review for accuracy? I want to avoid publishing outdated info that makes things worse.

Valid concern. Let's assign content ownership now. 561463, you own the overall content quality and publishing workflow (T6). But for each FAQ topic, we need a subject matter expert. 6370, since you're on the front lines, can you recommend who should own each category? For example, who in your team or elsewhere knows billing best?

Good question. For billing and invoices, that's usually handled by our finance team—I'd recommend reaching out to them. For password resets and account access, that's IT. Shipping and delivery is logistics. Returns and refunds is customer service (that's us, but we'd need to coordinate with returns). Subscription changes is product. I can help draft the initial content, but yeah, we need those teams to validate. Should we set up a review cycle?

Okay, so we need to loop in external stakeholders for review. That's a bit of a dependency. Let me propose: I'll draft the FAQs based on 6370's call notes and my understanding. Then we send them to the SMEs (finance, IT, logistics, product) for a 24-hour review window. If they don't respond, we publish with a caveat that it's subject to update. Does that work, or do we need formal sign-off from each team?

I think we need formal sign-off for accuracy-critical topics like billing and returns. But for general product info and troubleshooting, a 24-hour review is fine. Let me check with the stakeholders on the governance model. In the meantime, 561463, start drafting the FAQs for the top 5 categories. 6370, can you provide more detail on the most common questions within each category? Like, what exactly do people ask about billing?

Sure. For billing, the most common questions are: 'Why was I charged twice?', 'How do I get an invoice?', 'Can I change my billing date?', 'What payment methods do you accept?', 'Why was my payment declined?'. For password resets: 'I forgot my password', 'How do I reset my password?', 'I'm locked out of my account', 'Can I change my username?'. For shipping: 'Where's my order?', 'How long does shipping take?', 'Do you ship internationally?', 'What are shipping costs?'. I can send you the full list with call volumes for each question.

Perfect. That's exactly what I need. I'll draft answers for these and organize them by category. I'll also create a template for each FAQ so they're consistent in tone and structure. Should I include a 'last updated' date on each article so customers know it's current?

Yes, include a 'last updated' date. That builds trust. Also, add a 'Was this helpful?' feedback button at the bottom of each article. We'll use that data to identify which FAQs need improvement post-launch. 561463, can you have the first draft of 15 FAQs ready by day 8? That gives us time to review and iterate before we hit the content freeze on day 20.

Day 8 for 15 FAQs is doable. I'll prioritize the top 5 categories and get those out first. Then I'll move to the secondary topics. I'll also set up the content templates and workflow in A8 (Knowledge Base Governance and Workflow) so we have a clear process for updates post-launch.

I want to make sure we're thinking about the customer journey here. When a customer lands on the portal, they should be able to find answers quickly. 6370, from your experience, do customers usually know which category their question falls into? Or do they just search for keywords? That affects how we organize the FAQs.

Good point. Most customers just search for keywords or browse. They don't think in categories. So the search function is critical. If someone types 'where's my order', they should find the shipping FAQ immediately. And if they browse, the categories should be obvious—like 'Shipping & Delivery', 'Billing', 'Account & Access'. I think the category names matter a lot for discoverability.

That's useful for the IA. I'll make sure the category names are customer-friendly, not internal jargon. And I'll test the search and browse flows with a few sample questions to make sure they work intuitively.

Good. So let's confirm D3: the initial FAQ set for MVP includes the top 5 call driver categories (billing, account access, shipping, returns, subscriptions) with at least 3-5 FAQs per category, plus general product info and troubleshooting. That's roughly 20-25 FAQs by day 20. Does that align with what we discussed?
Yes, that's aligned. I'll prioritize those categories and make sure each FAQ is clear, accurate, and customer-friendly.
Looks good. I'll review the drafts for accuracy and make sure they match how we explain things on the phone.

Now for D4: content ownership. 561463 owns the overall content quality and publishing workflow. For each FAQ category, we need a subject matter expert. 6370, you'll own the support-side FAQs (returns, general product info, troubleshooting). For billing, account access, and shipping, we'll need to coordinate with finance, IT, and logistics. I'll reach out to those teams and confirm ownership by EOD tomorrow. Does that work?
Works for me. I'll make sure the support team is ready to maintain the FAQs after launch. We can do a quick training on the publishing workflow once 561463 has it set up.

I'll document the ownership and review process in A8 so it's clear who's responsible for what. And I'll set up a simple approval workflow—maybe a shared spreadsheet or a Slack bot—so updates don't get lost.

Perfect. So D3 and D4 are locked: initial FAQ set covers top 5 call drivers with 20-25 FAQs, and content ownership is assigned with 561463 as the overall owner and 6370 as the support-side SME. External SMEs (finance, IT, logistics) to be confirmed by EOD tomorrow. Let's move forward.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in information architecture, UX approach, and visual style.

messages.text: I've drafted the information architecture and wireframes for the self-service portal. Here's the structure: Home page with search bar and category tiles (Billing, Account & Access, Shipping, Returns, Subscriptions, General Info). FAQ page with category filters and search. How-to page with step-by-step guides. Contact page with escalation form. I've also created wireframes for mobile and desktop to ensure responsiveness. The design is clean and minimal—no heavy graphics, just clear typography and intuitive navigation. I've documented the user flows in A4 (Portal Information Architecture and User Flows). Please review and let me know if the structure makes sense for your use cases.

This looks solid. The category structure aligns with what we discussed in TH2. One question: on the FAQ page, can we add a 'Most Viewed' or 'Popular' section? That way, customers see the most helpful articles first without having to search. Also, I want to make sure the article layout has space for the 'last updated' date and 'Was this helpful?' feedback button we discussed.

Good ideas. I'll add a 'Popular' section on the FAQ page and include space for metadata (last updated, helpful button) on each article. I'll also add a breadcrumb trail so customers know where they are in the navigation. Let me update the wireframes and share them again by EOD today.

From a support perspective, this looks good. The categories match the call drivers we identified. One thing: can we add a 'Still need help?' section at the bottom of each article that links to the contact form? That way, if the FAQ doesn't answer the question, customers know how to escalate without getting frustrated.
Absolutely. I'll add that to every article. It's a good UX pattern for reducing frustration and enabling smooth escalation.

The wireframes are clear. I can start building the front-end once these are finalized. Just to confirm: are we using a CSS framework like Bootstrap, or custom CSS? And do we need to support older browsers, or can I assume modern browsers only?

Good questions. Use Bootstrap for consistency and speed. For browser support, assume modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge from the last 2 years). We need to support mobile (iOS and Android), so make sure the responsive design is solid. 75507, can you confirm the breakpoints and mobile-first approach in the wireframes?
Yes, I'm using mobile-first design. Breakpoints at 480px (mobile), 768px (tablet), and 1024px (desktop). The layout adapts smoothly across all sizes. I'll include that in the updated wireframes.

I want to flag accessibility early. The wireframes look clean, but we need to ensure: (1) color contrast meets WCAG AA standards, (2) all interactive elements are keyboard-accessible, (3) images have alt text, (4) form labels are properly associated. 75507, can you include an accessibility checklist in A3 (Content Style and Accessibility Guide) so we have a shared standard?

Good catch. I'll create a detailed accessibility checklist and include it in A3. I'll also test the wireframes with a screen reader to make sure the navigation is logical. And I'll use a color contrast checker to ensure all text meets WCAG AA standards.
I'll make sure all content follows the accessibility guidelines. For example, I'll use clear headings, short paragraphs, and simple language. And I'll avoid jargon that might confuse customers.

Accessibility is non-negotiable. It's part of our success metrics (zero critical accessibility gaps). 75507, once you finalize the wireframes with the accessibility checklist, we'll do a formal review before 448709 starts building. That's D6: confirm accessibility and mobile responsiveness requirements.
I'll have the updated wireframes with accessibility checklist ready by EOD today. Then we can review and finalize by tomorrow morning.
Now let's talk about visual style. 75507, can you share the style guide (colors, typography, components) that you mentioned? We need to lock that in so 448709 can build consistently.

I'm working on the style guide now. I'm using a neutral color palette (grays, blues, whites) with a single accent color (teal) for CTAs and highlights. Typography is clean and readable: sans-serif for headings, serif for body text. I'm also defining component styles for buttons, forms, cards, and modals. I'll include this in A3 along with the accessibility checklist. Should be ready by EOD today.
The color palette sounds good. Neutral and professional. I'll make sure the content tone matches—clear, helpful, and friendly. No corporate jargon.
Good. Once I have the style guide, I can start building the component library in Bootstrap. That'll speed up the front-end development.

Perfect. So D5 is: approve the navigation structure and key user flows from A4. The structure is: Home (search + categories) → FAQ (filters + search) → How-to (guides) → Contact (escalation). User flows for search, browse, and escalation are documented. Does everyone agree?
Agreed. The structure is intuitive and supports the content we're planning.
Looks good. Customers should be able to find answers quickly with this structure.
Confirmed. I'm ready to build.

Great. So D5 and D6 are locked: navigation structure approved, and accessibility/mobile responsiveness requirements confirmed. 75507, finalize the wireframes and style guide by EOD today. 448709, you can start the front-end build tomorrow morning. Let's keep the momentum.

threads.thread_goal: Confirm technical architecture, integrations, and analytics setup.

messages.text: I've drafted the technical architecture for the self-service portal. Here's the high-level design: (1) Front-end: responsive web app built with Bootstrap and vanilla JavaScript, hosted on our CDN. (2) Back-end: lightweight Node.js API for search and analytics, deployed on our existing infrastructure. (3) Database: PostgreSQL for knowledge base content, reusing our existing instance. (4) Authentication: public access for FAQ/search; optional integration with existing auth system for future features. (5) CRM integration: read-only access to pull customer data for analytics. (6) Analytics: custom event tracking for portal usage, search queries, and estimated call deflection. I've documented this in A5 (Technical Architecture and Integration Plan). The approach minimizes new infrastructure and reuses existing systems. Let me know if you see any risks or dependencies.

This looks reasonable. A few questions: (1) For the search functionality, are we using a full-text search engine like Elasticsearch, or just SQL queries? (2) For the analytics, are we sending data to a third-party service or storing it in our own database? (3) What's the expected traffic volume, and do we need to worry about scaling?

Good questions. (1) For MVP, we'll use PostgreSQL full-text search. It's simple and sufficient for 25-30 FAQs. If we scale later, we can migrate to Elasticsearch. (2) Analytics: we'll store events in our own database and build a simple dashboard. No third-party service for now. (3) Traffic: we're expecting moderate load initially (maybe 1000-2000 unique visitors per day). Our current infrastructure can handle that. If we hit 10k+ visitors, we'll need to optimize, but that's a good problem to have. Does that address your concerns?

Makes sense. PostgreSQL full-text search is fine for MVP. I'll implement the search functionality in T9 (Implement search and FAQ filtering). For the analytics, I'll set up event tracking on key actions: page views, search queries, article clicks, contact form submissions. That should give us enough data to measure deflection.

Perfect. Now let's talk about the CRM integration. We need to pull customer data for analytics—specifically, which customers viewed the portal and which articles they accessed. This helps us estimate call deflection. I'll work with the CRM team to set up a read-only API. 448709, once I have the API spec, can you integrate it into the analytics pipeline?
Yes, I can do that. Just send me the API spec and I'll integrate it. How soon do you think you'll have that?

I'll reach out to the CRM team today and aim to have the spec by day 3. That gives you time to integrate before we start testing. Now, let's talk about analytics and reporting. I'll set up a dashboard (A7: Portal Analytics and Call Deflection Dashboard) that tracks: (1) daily unique visitors, (2) most viewed articles, (3) search queries and click-through rates, (4) contact form submissions, (5) estimated call deflection (based on article views and support ticket reduction). We'll review this dashboard weekly post-launch.
Good. For the deflection metric, how are we calculating it? Are we comparing support ticket volume before and after launch, or are we using a proxy metric like 'articles viewed per unique visitor'?

Good point. We'll use both. Primary metric: compare support ticket volume 30 days before launch vs. 30 days after. Secondary metric: track articles viewed per unique visitor and estimate deflection based on historical call patterns. For example, if 100 customers view the 'password reset' FAQ, and we know that 'password reset' calls are 15% of inbound volume, we can estimate that we deflected ~15 calls. It's not perfect, but it gives us a directional estimate.

That makes sense. Just make sure we're transparent about the methodology so stakeholders understand the limitations. And let's plan a post-launch review meeting (maybe day 7 or 14) to discuss early results and iterate if needed.

Absolutely. I'll schedule a post-launch review for day 7 to check early metrics and identify any quick wins or issues. Now, let's confirm D7: approve the technical architecture and integration approach. The architecture is: public-facing front-end (Bootstrap + JavaScript), Node.js API for search and analytics, PostgreSQL for content, read-only CRM integration for analytics, and a custom dashboard for reporting. Does everyone agree?
Agreed. I can build the front-end and integrate the search/analytics with this architecture.
Confirmed. The architecture is sound and minimizes risk by reusing existing systems.

Great. Now for D8: agree on the analytics events and reporting cadence. Events to track: (1) page views, (2) search queries, (3) article clicks, (4) contact form submissions, (5) time on page. Reporting cadence: weekly dashboard review post-launch, with a formal metrics review on day 7 and day 30. Does that work?
Good. I'd also suggest we track 'search queries with zero results' so we can identify gaps in our FAQ coverage. That's a quick way to find topics we need to add post-launch.

Excellent idea. I'll add that to the analytics. So D8 is confirmed: track page views, search queries (including zero-result queries), article clicks, contact submissions, and time on page. Weekly dashboard review, formal metrics review on day 7 and day 30. 448709, can you have the analytics integration ready by day 15 so we can test it before launch?
Day 15 is tight, but I can do it. I'll prioritize the analytics integration after the front-end and search are done. Should be ready for testing by day 15.

Perfect. So D7 and D8 are locked: technical architecture approved, and analytics events and reporting cadence confirmed. Let's keep moving. I'll reach out to the CRM team today for the API spec. 448709, start the front-end build tomorrow. We're on track for day 30 launch.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pre-launch checks, training, and go-live date.

messages.text: We're at day 15 and it's time to plan the final push to launch. I've drafted a pre-launch checklist (A6: Pre-Launch Content and UX Review Checklist) that covers: (1) content accuracy and completeness, (2) broken links and formatting, (3) UX walkthrough with real users, (4) accessibility compliance check, (5) analytics validation, (6) support team training and readiness. I've also outlined the knowledge base governance workflow (A8: Knowledge Base Governance and Workflow) so we have a clear process for maintaining content post-launch. Let me walk through the checklist and timeline. We have 15 days left, so we need to be disciplined about what we test and when.

Good. Let's break down the timeline. Days 15-20: finalize content, complete UX walkthrough, run accessibility audit. Days 20-25: fix critical issues, validate analytics, prepare training materials. Days 25-30: final testing, support team training, go-live. Does that align with where we are on each workstream?

From the content side, I'm on track. I have 22 FAQs drafted and reviewed by 6370. I'm working on the final 3-5 how-to guides. By day 18, all content will be ready for the UX walkthrough. I'll also finalize the content templates and governance workflow by day 16 so we have a clear process for post-launch updates.

From the design side, I'm done with the wireframes and style guide. 448709 is building the front-end now. I'll do a UX walkthrough with the team by day 18 to catch any usability issues before we go live. I'll also run the accessibility audit by day 20.

I'm on track with the front-end build. I have the home page and FAQ page mostly done. I'm working on the search functionality and contact form now. By day 18, the front-end should be feature-complete. Then I'll focus on bug fixes and performance optimization through day 25.

From the architecture side, I'm integrating the CRM API and setting up the analytics dashboard. By day 15, the analytics should be live and collecting data. By day 20, I'll have the dashboard ready for review. By day 25, we'll validate that the deflection metrics are accurate.

From the support side, I'm ready to review content and help with training. I'll also coordinate with the support manager to schedule the team training for day 27-28. That gives us a couple of days to address any questions before go-live on day 30.

I'll prepare the training materials and quick-reference guide (T11) by day 22. That gives us time to review with 6370 and the support manager before the training sessions. I'll also create a simple FAQ for the support team—'How do I use the portal to help customers?'—so they can reference it during calls.

One thing I want to flag: the pre-launch checklist includes a content accuracy review. I'll need 6370 and the external SMEs (finance, IT, logistics) to sign off on their respective FAQs by day 18. That's tight, but doable if we send them the drafts today.
I'll send the SME drafts today and ask for sign-off by day 17. That gives us a day to fix any issues before the UX walkthrough. 561463, can you coordinate the review process?

Yes, I'll send the drafts to the SMEs today with a clear deadline of day 17. I'll also prepare a feedback form so they can comment directly on the content. Once I have their feedback, I'll incorporate it and finalize the FAQs by day 18.

For the UX walkthrough, I want to test the portal with a few real users—maybe 3-5 customers from different segments. That way we can catch usability issues before launch. Can we recruit some beta testers by day 16?
I can help recruit beta testers from our customer base. I'll reach out to a few loyal customers and ask if they'd be willing to test the portal. Should be easy to get 5-10 volunteers by day 16.

Great. I'll prepare a simple test script and feedback form for the beta testers. We'll ask them to complete a few tasks (search for an answer, browse FAQs, contact support) and give us feedback on usability and clarity. By day 19, I'll have the results and we can prioritize fixes.

Now let's talk about the go-live date. We have 15 days left. If we stick to the timeline, we can launch on day 30. But I want to build in a buffer. What if we aim for day 28 and use days 28-30 as a 'soft launch' window where we monitor closely and fix any critical issues? That way, if something goes wrong, we have time to roll back or patch.

I like that idea. A soft launch gives us time to catch issues without the pressure of a hard deadline. We can promote the portal gradually—first to the support team, then to a subset of customers, then to everyone. That also gives us time to iterate on content based on early feedback.
A soft launch makes sense. It gives me time to fix bugs without rushing. I can have the portal feature-complete by day 25, then spend days 25-28 on testing and optimization.
A soft launch also gives us time to monitor the UX in production. We can see how real users interact with the portal and make final tweaks if needed.

Good. So the timeline is: days 15-20 finalize content and design, days 20-25 complete front-end and analytics, days 25-28 soft launch (internal + beta customers), days 28-30 monitor and fix issues, day 30 full launch. Now, let's confirm D1 (reconfirm MVP scope) and D4 (validate content owners are ready). For D1, the MVP scope is locked: responsive web UI, 25+ FAQs, 10+ how-to guides, search/filtering, contact escalation, analytics dashboard, support training. Non-MVP items are parked. Does everyone agree?
Confirmed. The MVP scope is clear and achievable.
Confirmed.
Confirmed.

Now for D4: validate that content owners are ready to maintain articles after launch. 561463, you own the overall content quality and publishing workflow. 6370, you own the support-side FAQs. External SMEs (finance, IT, logistics) own their respective categories. Are you all ready to commit to maintaining the content post-launch? This includes reviewing articles monthly, updating outdated info, and responding to feedback.

Yes, I'm ready. I'll own the publishing workflow and coordinate with the SMEs on updates. I'll also monitor the analytics for zero-result searches and identify gaps in our FAQ coverage. I'll schedule a monthly content review meeting with the team to discuss updates and improvements.
I'm ready. I'll review the support-side FAQs monthly and flag any outdated info. I'll also monitor customer feedback from the portal and suggest new FAQ topics based on what customers are asking.

Perfect. So D1 and D4 are confirmed: MVP scope is locked and reconfirmed, and content owners are ready to maintain articles post-launch. 561463, finalize the pre-launch checklist (A6) and governance workflow (A8) by day 16. 6370, coordinate with the support manager on training schedule for days 27-28. 59590, finalize the training materials (T11) by day 22. Let's execute the final push.
I'll have the training materials ready by day 22. I'll also prepare a post-launch support plan so the team knows how to handle issues during the soft launch and full launch.

Excellent. We're on track for a day 28 soft launch and day 30 full launch. Let's keep the momentum and execute the final push. Daily standups starting tomorrow to track progress and blockers. See you all tomorrow.
